content: Animals were initially sent into space to evaluate the survivability of spaceflight before human missions were attempted. Over time, animals were also used to study biological processes and the effects of microgravity and space travel on living organisms. Five national space programs—those of the United States, the Soviet Union, France, Japan, and China—have launched animals into space. In 1947, a V-2 rocket was launched to study the effects of radiation exposure at high altitudes. Subsequent V-2 missions carried biological samples, including moss. After the failure of the first Albert mission, Albert II, a rhesus monkey, was launched but died on impact due to a parachute failure. During the 1950s and 1960s, monkeys were implanted with sensors to monitor vital signs, and many were anesthetized during launch. In 1949, a mouse was launched aboard a V-2 rocket, reaching an altitude of 137 km. This flight, part of the Albert V mission, did not include a monkey. Several other mice were launched in the 1950s, but only the first mouse survived. On January 29, 1951, the Soviet Union launched the R-1 IIIA-1 flight, carrying two dogs, Tsygan (Gypsy) and Dezik, into space, though not into orbit. Later that year, mice were launched aboard spacecraft, but they failed to reach the altitude required for true spaceflight. The first animal to orbit Earth was the Soviet dog Laika, aboard Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957. Laika died during the flight. At least 10 other dogs were launched into orbit, and many others were sent on suborbital flights before Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961. On December 13, 1958, a Jupiter IRBM (AM-13) was launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying a squirrel monkey named Gordo. Unfortunately, the recovery parachute failed, and Gordo was lost. Telemetry data showed that Gordo survived the 10 g forces of launch, 8 minutes of weightlessness, and 40 g forces during reentry at 10,000 mph. The nose cone sank 1,302 nautical miles downrange and was not recovered. In 1959, monkeys Able and Baker became the first monkeys to survive spaceflight. Able, a 7-pound rhesus monkey, and Baker, an 11-ounce squirrel monkey, were launched to an altitude of 360 miles and traveled 1,700 miles downrange. They endured forces 38 times the pull of gravity and experienced 9 minutes of weightlessness. Their flight reached a top speed of 10,000 mph and lasted 16 minutes. Able died four days later due to complications from surgery to remove an infected electrode, while Baker lived until November 29, 1984. On January 31, 1961, Ham the chimpanzee was launched aboard a Mercury capsule on a Redstone rocket as part of the Mercury-Redstone 2 mission. Ham had been trained to pull levers to receive banana pellet rewards and avoid electric shocks. His flight demonstrated the ability to perform tasks during spaceflight. A few months later, Alan Shepard became the first American in space. On November 29, 1961, Enos the chimp became the first non-human primate to orbit Earth aboard a Mercury capsule on the Mercury-Atlas 5 mission. In March 1961, the Soviet Union launched mice, guinea pigs, and frogs (Northern Leopard Frogs) aboard the Vostok 3A flights. France launched the first rat into space on February 22, 1961, followed by two more rats in October 1962. On October 18, 1963, France launched Felix the cat into space, equipped with electrodes implanted in its head to measure neural impulses. Felix was recovered alive, but the next cat launched did not survive. France's final animal launches in March 1967 included two monkeys. China launched mice and rats in 1964 and 1965, and two dogs in 1966. On February 22, 1966, the Soviet Union launched two dogs, Veterok (Little Wind) and Ugolyok (Ember), aboard Voskhod 3. They spent 22 days in orbit, a record for dogs that was not surpassed by humans until Skylab 2 in 1974. The United States launched Biosatellite I in 1966 and Biosatellite II in 1967, carrying fruit flies, parasitic wasps, flour beetles, frog eggs, bacteria, amoebae, plants, and fungi. The first tortoise in space, a Horsfield's tortoise, was launched by the Soviet Union on September 14, 1968, on a circumlunar voyage with wine flies, mealworms, and other biological specimens. The capsule was recovered at sea on September 21. In the 1970s, two bullfrogs were launched on a one-way mission aboard the Orbiting Frog Otolith satellite on November 9, 1970, to study space motion sickness. Apollo 16 (April 16, 1972) carried nematodes, and Apollo 17 (December 7, 1972) carried five pocket mice, one of which died during the circumlunar trip. Skylab 3 carried pocket mice, the first fish in space (a mummichog), and the first spiders in space (cross spiders named Arabella and Anita). The Apollo-Soyuz mission also flew mummichogs. The Soviet Union's Bion program launched tortoises, rats, and mummichogs on various missions. Salyut 5 (June 22, 1976) carried tortoises and a zebra danio fish. In the 1980s, experiments included chicken embryos (fertilized eggs) sent into space on STS-29 in 1989 as part of a student contest. Earlier shuttle missions included projects involving ants, stick insect eggs, and brine shrimp cysts. In the 1990s, the last Bion flights of the Soviet Union carried monkeys, frogs, and fruit flies. The Foton program carried dormant brine shrimp, newts, fruit flies, and desert beetles. China launched guinea pigs in 1990. Japanese journalist Toyohiro Akiyama brought Japanese tree frogs to the Mir space station in December 1990. Other biological experiments aboard Mir involved quail eggs. Japan launched its first animals, a species of newt, into space on March 18, 1995. The Space Shuttle Columbia carried a variety of animals, including crickets, mice, rats, frogs, newts, fruit flies, snails, carp, medaka, oyster toadfish, sea urchins, swordtail fish, gypsy moth eggs, stick insect eggs, and quail eggs. In the 2000s, the final flight of Columbia in 2003 carried silkworms, golden orb spiders, carpenter bees, harvester ants, and Japanese killifish. Nematodes (C. elegans) from one experiment were found alive in the debris after the Columbia disaster. C. elegans were also part of experiments aboard the International Space Station, along with research involving quail eggs. Earlier shuttle missions included student projects with ants, stick insect eggs, and brine shrimp cysts. On July 12, 2006, Bigelow Aerospace launched Genesis I, an inflatable space module containing small items, including insects, chosen by company employees. These included Madagascar hissing cockroaches and Mexican jumping beans (seeds containing live moth larvae). On June 28, 2007, Bigelow launched Genesis II, which carried the same cockroaches and added South African flat rock scorpions and seed-harvester ants.
